flashcards.a: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy.

flashcards.q: Distinguish Adapter from Facade in one line each.
flashcards.a: Adapter translates one interface into another (1-to-1 compatibility, usually one vendor). Facade simplifies access to a subsystem of multiple components behind one simpler interface (many-to-one simplicity).

flashcards.q: Distinguish Decorator from Proxy in one line each.
flashcards.a: Decorator keeps the same interface and ADDS behavior, meant to stack arbitrarily. Proxy keeps the same interface and CONTROLS access (lazy load, permission check, rate limit) -- the real object may not even be created yet.

flashcards.q: Why is a Facade with 40 public methods and business logic inside it a red flag?
flashcards.a: It has stopped being a thin delegation layer and become a God Object wearing a Facade's name. A proper facade mostly delegates to well-scoped subsystem components rather than containing its own conditionals and state.

flashcards.q: Why does decorator stacking order matter?
flashcards.a: Decorator composition is not commutative. E.g. @logged over @cached logs every call including cache hits; reversed, cache hits never reach the logger. Outermost decorator sees the call first and the result last.

flashcards.q: What is the classic failure mode of an ORM lazy-loading Proxy?
flashcards.a: N+1 query storm: iterating over N records and accessing a lazily-proxied relation on each triggers N separate round-trip queries. Fix with explicit eager loading (joinedload/selectinload/Preload) on hot paths.

flashcards.q: When is Composite the right tool versus a flat list with a type tag?
flashcards.a: When data is genuinely recursive (a rule can contain other rules, a folder can contain files or folders) and callers need to operate on the whole structure uniformly without branching on depth or type -- every node, leaf or branch, implements the same interface.

flashcards.q: What is the actual trigger condition for using Bridge, and how does it differ from Strategy?
flashcards.a: Bridge is justified only when 2 independent hierarchies both need to vary, avoiding an NxM subclass explosion (N shapes x M renderers). Structurally near-identical to Strategy; the difference is intent -- Bridge prevents combinatorial explosion across two hierarchies, Strategy swaps one algorithm.

flashcards.q: Why is Flyweight rarely needed explicitly in Python or the JVM?
flashcards.a: Both runtimes already flyweight common primitives automatically -- Python caches small integers (-5 to 256) and interns some strings; the JVM has a string pool and caches boxed Integers in the same range. A hand-built pool is worth it only for larger domain objects under measured memory pressure.

flashcards.q: Rank the 7 structural patterns by real-world frequency in backend services.
flashcards.a: Most common: Decorator, Proxy, Adapter, Facade (every middleware, ORM lazy-load, vendor SDK wrapper, service API). Situational: Composite (genuinely recursive domains). Rare: Bridge, Flyweight (GUI toolkits, driver layers, extreme object-count memory pressure).

flashcards.q: What does isolating a third-party SDK behind an Adapter actually buy you, measurably?
flashcards.a: When the vendor changes their API, the blast radius is confined to the one adapter file instead of every call site -- turning what could be a dangerous multi-file refactor into a single-file change.

flashcards.q: Is Python's @decorator syntax always the GoF Decorator pattern?
flashcards.a: No. Behavior-wrapping decorators (@retry, @cached) are the GoF pattern. Metadata/registration decorators (@app.route, @dataclass) are closer to reflection/registration and don't wrap behavior around the call at all -- conflating the two is a common but incorrect simplification.

flashcards.q: What is Envoy's sidecar proxy, in GoF pattern terms?
flashcards.a: An infrastructure-scale Proxy (transparent stand-in controlling access to the real service) that also adds cross-cutting Decorator-style behavior (retries, mTLS, observability) -- the same Proxy/Decorator ambiguity seen in application-level caching wrappers, at network scale.
